articles.title: SJAA EPHEMERIS
articles.summary: This document is the "SJAA EPHEMERIS," the official publication of the San Jose Astronomical Association, specifically Volume 3, Number 3, from March 1992. It represents a historical issue of the association's regular periodical.

articles.title: To The Members of the SJAA
articles.summary: Denni Medlock and Kevin express deep gratitude to the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) and friends for their support after losing their home and telescope collection in the Oakland fire. The SJAA replaced their lost Gregory Awards, and various gifts like eyepieces and books were received, highlighting the overwhelming generosity and community spirit that aided their recovery.

articles.title: FREMONT PEAK STAR PARTY
articles.summary: This article details a star party held at Fremont Peak on January 25, 1992, where attendees gathered despite initial overcast skies that later cleared for some viewing before fog set in. Participants, including Paul Barton and Jim Baggott, socialized despite a telescope's electronic issues and limited viewing conditions. The document also provides a comprehensive calendar of upcoming astronomical events for March and April 1992, including star parties, general meetings, and astronomy classes.

articles.title: THE EYEPIECE
articles.summary: The article announces an upcoming club meeting featuring Shilo, who will speak about the history of Lick Observatory. It primarily discusses an ongoing observatory project at Grant Ranch, urging members to actively participate and provide input to the Board of Directors and Del Johnson. The project aims to establish an observatory, potentially alongside Halls Valley's, for public educational service, requiring collaboration with the Park Planning Commission.

articles.title: Dr. Clyde Tombaugh's talk to the EAS
articles.summary: Dr. Clyde Tombaugh's 1989 talk to the EAS details his groundbreaking discovery of Pluto, illustrating its orbital motion and the impressive accuracy of Percival Lowell's prediction despite the planet's small mass. He shares insights into other discoveries made during his extensive sky survey, such as a supercluster of galaxies, and the observational challenges posed by dense star fields, also touching upon the later discovery of Pluto's moon, Charon, and how World War II curtailed his broader celestial search.

articles.title: Cure For Horizon Envy
articles.summary: This article captures a conversation between two amateur astronomers, one in the Northern and one in the Southern Hemisphere, discussing their mutual "horizon envy" for celestial objects hidden from their respective views. Alex, from the Southern Hemisphere, vividly describes the incredible naked-eye and telescopic views of objects like the Magellanic Clouds, 47 Tucanae, and the Eta Carinae Nebula, particularly from dark sky locations. The exchange highlights the unique astronomical treasures available from different latitudes and the shared desire to observe them, concluding that the sky is always starrier on the other side of the celestial equator.

articles.title: CELESTIAL CALENDAR
articles.summary: This document provides a detailed celestial calendar for the month of March, outlining key astronomical events and data. It includes lunar phases with their dates, rise, transit, and set times, along with similar information for the nearer planets (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) and their magnitudes/distances. Additionally, it provides solar data, astronomical twilight times, sidereal time, and highlights the darkest night for observation.

articles.title: TIMES AND DATES ARE PACIFIC STANDARD
articles.summary: This document highlights the perceived lack of major astronomical events and a low membership count for organizations like ALPO and BAA in the Southern Hemisphere, particularly Australia. It extends an invitation for increased participation in the region's astronomical community. The content appears to be an excerpt, likely from an ephemeris or newsletter dated March 1992.

articles.title: FEBRUARY 1 GRANT RANCH STAR PARTY
articles.summary: Paul Barton reported on the February 1st Grant Ranch Star Party, detailing the cold and wet weather conditions that caused most participants to depart by midnight. Despite the challenging conditions, numerous individuals attended with a variety of telescopes, including large Dobsonians and SCTs, for an evening of observation. The report also lists several attendees and their equipment, highlighting the continued effort to organize and document such community astronomy events.

articles.title: FEBRUARY 2 FREMONT PEAK STAR PARTY
articles.summary: A star party held on February 2nd at Fremont Peak experienced clear but cold and wet conditions, with excellent seeing for observing the winter Milky Way and R Monocerotis. Attendees utilized homemade Dobsonian telescopes, and a park ranger's intervention was necessary to quiet noisy campers disrupting the astronomers. Despite the challenges, the viewing was good but physically tiring.

articles.title: SJAA OBSERVATORY
articles.summary: The SJAA Observatory project at Grant Ranch County Park is progressing with the formation of a site survey team tasked with locating Halley Hill, mapping the site, and assessing the existing trail. This groundwork, conducted in coordination with park staff, is crucial before observatory design can commence. Members are also being solicited for a "wish list" of features and to contribute to developing design concepts for the observatory.

articles.title: MOUNT LEMON OBSERVATORY ASTRONOMY CAMPS
articles.summary: Bill Dellinges recounts his exceptionally positive experience at a novice adult astronomy camp hosted by the University of Arizona's Mount Lemon Observatory. He praises the dedication and generosity of the staff, led by Dr. Don McCarthy, who ensured participants had an immersive and educational three-day experience. The camp, operated through the Arizona Alumni Association, offers both adult and children's programs throughout the year.

articles.title: Group 70 Friday Jan 17,1992
articles.summary: On January 17-18, 1992, Group 70 members successfully installed a 1.8-meter glass mirror blank onto a grinding machine after extensive preparation and safety checks. This milestone event saw the initial grinding begin, breaking the virgin surface of the blank. The article concludes with an urgent call for volunteers and financial support to continue the ambitious telescope-making project.

articles.title: HOW MANY OF YOU CAUGHT THE FEBRUARY MISTAKE? FIRST PAGE FOR THOSE WHO DIDN'T. IT REALLY WAS FEB - NOT JAN! SORRY!
articles.summary: This article is an apology and correction for a previous error where the month February was mistakenly identified as January in an earlier publication. It directs readers to page 5, which contains the correct Ephemeris for March 1992.

articles.title: Comet Comments
articles.summary: The article "Comet Comments" by Don Machholz announces the recent discoveries of Comet Helin-Alu (1992a) and Comet Bradfield (1992b), detailing their discovery circumstances, magnitudes, and orbital parameters. It also provides brief updates on the status and projected visibility of Comet Shoemaker-Levy (1991d) and Comet Mueller.

articles.title: Offices and Board of Directors
articles.summary: This document presents the contact information for an organization's Board of Directors, officers, and ephemeris contributors, along with the editor's details. It also includes an account of an astronomy trip that involved visiting Mt. Lemon and Mt. Bigelow Observatories, where participants used various telescopes for deep-sky viewing and observed the Hubble Space Telescope. The trip concluded with an optional tour of Kitt Peak Observatory, highlighting facilities like the McMath Solar Telescope and Mayall reflector.

articles.title: EPHEMERIDES
articles.summary: This document provides detailed ephemerides for two comets, Shoemaker-Levy (1991d) and Mueller (1991h₁), covering dates from late February to early April. For each comet, it lists daily celestial coordinates (RA, DEC), elongation from the sun, sky visibility (morning/evening), and predicted visual magnitude, offering a guide for observers.

articles.title: ASTRO ADS
articles.summary: The "ASTRO ADS" section serves as a classifieds board for free, noncommercial listings of astronomically related products and services, detailing submission guidelines and deadlines. It features numerous advertisements for various telescopes (e.g., Celestron C14, C5, C8, C10), eyepieces, astrophotography equipment, mounts, and computer systems, along with contact information and prices. Additionally, the document announces the National Astronomy Expo and provides a positive review and contact details for an astronomy seminar/camp offered by the University of Arizona Alumni Association.

articles.title: EPHEMERIS
articles.summary: EPHEMERIS is a monthly publication by the San Jose Astronomical Association, providing its address. Members are encouraged to submit typed articles for publication by the 12th of the previous month, with submissions directed to editor Bob Madden at a specified address.

articles.title: SAN JOSE ASTRONOMICAL ASSOCIATION MEMBERSHIP
articles.summary: This document is a membership application form for the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA). It outlines different membership tiers, including individual, membership with Sky & Telescope magazine, and junior memberships, along with their respective costs. The form provides instructions for submission, either at an SJAA meeting or by mail to the treasurer, and requests payment via check.

articles.title: SJAA HOTLINE
articles.summary: This document snippet provides the 24-hour hotline number for the SJAA (San Jose Astronomical Association) for information. It also indicates that ephemeris data for March 1992 is available, likely as part of a larger publication or service.
